lessons.title: Writing about context
lessons.summary: Learn what counts as context, build a bank of useful contextual ideas for each set text, and master the techniques for weaving context into analysis so that it earns AO3 marks instead of sitting on the side.
objectives: I can explain what AO3 assesses and the different kinds of context that count.
I can recall the most useful contextual ideas for Macbeth, A Christmas Carol, An Inspector Calls and the poetry cluster.
I can integrate context into a paragraph so that it explains a writer's choice or a reader's response.
I can distinguish between the context of when a text was written and when it is read.
I can avoid common context errors: bolt-ons, biography dumps, generalisations and anachronism.

activities.title: What context is, and what AO3 rewards
activities.content:
## The relationship, not the facts

AO3 asks you to *show understanding of the relationship between texts and the contexts in which they were written*. The word to underline is **relationship**. A fact about the past is not context until it is connected to a **choice the writer made** or a **response the reader has**.

## Kinds of context that count

| Type | Examples | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical** | The Gunpowder Plot; the 1834 Poor Law; the two world wars | Explains why an idea felt urgent |
| **Social** | Class hierarchy; the position of women; attitudes to poverty | Explains how characters treat one another |
| **Religious and philosophical** | Divine Right of Kings; Christian ideas of redemption; socialism; Romanticism | Explains a text's values |
| **Literary** | Tragedy; the ghost story; the well-made play; the sonnet | Explains form and expectations |
| **Biographical** | Dickens's childhood; Owen's service; Priestley's broadcasts | Explains a writer's purpose (use sparingly) |
| **Reception** | How a 1606 audience, a 1945 audience or a modern reader responds | Explains changing meanings |

## Two contexts for every text

- The **context of production**: when and why it was written.
- The **context of reception**: when it is read or performed, including now.

The gap between them is often where the best AO3 points live. *An Inspector Calls* is set in 1912, written in 1945 and watched today, and each layer changes what Birling's confidence means.

**Remember:** AO3 is 6 of 30 marks on the main essays and is **not assessed** on unseen poetry. Brief, precise, integrated context beats long contextual paragraphs every time.

activities.title: Bolt-on versus integrated: three pairs
activities.content:
**Macbeth**

*Bolt-on:* James I was king when the play was written and he believed in witches.

*Integrated:* Shakespeare gives the witches the first word of the play, a choice that would have unsettled an audience whose king had written a treatise on witchcraft and who took demonic influence seriously; their opening chant makes the supernatural the frame through which every later event is seen.

**A Christmas Carol**

*Bolt-on:* In Victorian times many people were poor and there were workhouses.

*Integrated:* Scrooge's question about whether the workhouses are still in operation is chilling precisely because the 1834 Poor Law had made them deliberately harsh; Dickens lets his miser treat a punishment as a charity so that readers who shared that complacency would hear it in Scrooge's voice.

**Power and Conflict**

*Bolt-on:* Wilfred Owen fought in the First World War and died in 1918.

*Integrated:* Owen's refrain that nothing happens draws on his own winter in the trenches in 1917, and its flat repetition rejects the heroic language of earlier war poetry, which a public raised on Tennyson would still have expected.

**The pattern in every integrated version:** a **quotation or choice** → the **context** that explains it → the **effect** on the original or modern audience.

activities.title: A context bank for each text
activities.content:
## Macbeth (c. 1606)

- **James I**: Scottish king, descended (supposedly) from Banquo; wrote *Daemonologie* on witchcraft; survived the **Gunpowder Plot** of 1605. The play flatters him (Banquo's line of kings) and dramatises the horror of killing a king.
- **Divine Right of Kings**: the monarch is God's deputy; regicide is a crime against heaven and nature (hence the storms and unnatural events after Duncan's death).
- **The Great Chain of Being**: everything has its place; ambition that disrupts the order brings chaos.
- **Gender**: expectations of masculinity as violence and of women as gentle; Lady Macbeth's *"unsex me here"* attacks those expectations.
- **Tragedy**: a great man with a fatal flaw; the audience expects a fall.

## A Christmas Carol (1843)

- The **Hungry Forties**; the **1834 Poor Law** and workhouses; **Malthus** and *surplus population*.
- Dickens's own **childhood poverty**; his visit to a **Ragged School**; his belief in **education** and practical **Christian charity**.
- The **revival of Christmas**; the **ghost story** tradition; the **carol** form.

## An Inspector Calls (written 1945, set 1912)

- **1912**: Edwardian class hierarchy; strikes; women without the vote; no welfare state; the Titanic.
- **1945**: two world wars; Priestley's **socialism** and wartime broadcasts; the Labour landslide and the **welfare state**.
- **Forms**: the well-made play; the morality play; the detective story.

## Power and Conflict

- **Romanticism** (Shelley, Wordsworth, Blake): nature, imagination, distrust of tyranny and institutions.
- **Victorian empire and honour** (Tennyson, Browning): duty, hierarchy, control.
- **First World War** (Owen); its long shadow (Hughes); modern conflicts and trauma (Armitage, Weir, Duffy); exile, colonialism and identity (Rumens, Agard, Dharker, Garland).

Learn **three or four** points per text. Depth of use beats breadth of knowledge.

activities.title: Techniques for weaving context in
activities.content:
## Five ways to integrate

**1. The 'so that' move.** State the writer's choice, then the context, then the purpose: *Shakespeare has Banquo's descendants appear as a line of kings so that James I, who claimed descent from Banquo, sees his own dynasty blessed on stage.*

**2. The 'would have' move.** Describe the original audience's likely response: *A Jacobean audience would have heard Macbeth's promise to jump the life to come as a terrifying gamble with his soul.*

**3. The 'then and now' move.** Compare receptions: *Where Victorian readers may have seen Scrooge's transformation as a Christian conversion, a modern reader is more likely to read it as a political argument about welfare.*

**4. The 'writer's purpose' move.** Attach biography to intention, briefly: *Dickens, who had seen the Ragged Schools for himself, makes Ignorance the more dangerous child.*

**5. The 'form' move.** Use literary context: *By writing a dramatic monologue, Browning uses a Victorian form designed to let a speaker condemn himself.*

## Sentence starters

- *Writing in..., the poet...*
- *For an audience who had just lived through..., this line...*
- *The play's original audience would have recognised...*
- *This reflects the contemporary belief that...*
- *Dickens challenges the widespread assumption that...*

## Placement

Put context **after** your analysis of a quotation, where it explains the effect, or **in the topic sentence** where it frames the point. One or two sentences per paragraph, in two or three paragraphs, is plenty for full AO3 marks.

activities.title: A model paragraph with integrated context
activities.content:
**Question:** How does Shakespeare present the witches as a dangerous influence?

> Shakespeare presents the witches as dangerous not because they force Macbeth to act but because they tell him a truth he wants to hear. Their greeting, *"All hail, Macbeth, that shalt be King hereafter!"*, is a prophecy without an instruction: they never say how or when, and this silence is what Macbeth fills with murder. Banquo sees the danger at once, warning that *"the instruments of darkness tell us truths"* in order to betray us *"in deepest consequence"*. For Shakespeare's audience, this was more than a plot point. King James had written *Daemonologie* to argue that witches were real servants of the devil whose purpose was to tempt the godly into damnation, and the play stages exactly that process: a good soldier led to regicide by a half-truth. By giving the witches equivocal language rather than direct commands, Shakespeare both satisfies a king who feared them and makes a subtler point that would still unsettle a modern audience, that the most dangerous voice is the one that only confirms what we already desire.

**Where the context sits:** after the analysis of the quotations, explaining why the equivocation would have frightened a Jacobean audience, and then extended to a modern response. Two sentences; fully integrated.

activities.title: Pitfalls
activities.content:
## Six ways context goes wrong

**1. The bolt-on.** A fact dropped between two sentences of analysis with no connection. Test: can it be deleted without loss? If yes, rewrite it as a *so that* sentence.

**2. The biography dump.** A paragraph on the writer's life. The examiner is marking your reading of the text, not your knowledge of the author. Use biography only to explain **purpose**, in one sentence.

**3. The generalisation.** *All Victorians were religious.* *Everyone in 1606 believed in witches.* Real societies disagree with themselves. Prefer *many*, *most* or *the play's original audience would largely have...*

**4. The anachronism.** Judging characters by ideas that did not exist yet, or claiming a writer was responding to events after their death. Check dates: *A Christmas Carol* (1843) cannot respond to Darwin (1859).

**5. The over-claim.** *Shakespeare wrote Macbeth to warn James I about ambition.* We rarely know intentions; say *the play could be read as...* or *Shakespeare seems to...*

**6. The wrong place.** Context in an unseen poetry answer earns nothing and wastes minutes. Invented context (*the poet probably lost her father*) looks like guesswork.

## A quick self-test

For each context sentence, ask three questions:
- Which **quotation or choice** does it explain?
- What **effect** on the original or modern audience does it account for?
- Is it **specific** (a date, a law, a belief) rather than vague (*back then*)?

Three yeses, and the sentence is earning its place.

question.text: True or false: writing 'everyone in Shakespeare's time believed in witches' is a safe contextual claim.
question.hint: Think about whether any society is completely united in its beliefs.
question.explanation: False. It is a generalisation. Some Jacobeans were sceptical about witchcraft. Prefer 'many in Shakespeare's audience' or 'the king himself believed', which is accurate and specific.

options.text: True
False

question.text:
A student writes: *"Lady Macbeth says 'unsex me here'. In Shakespeare's time women were expected to be gentle and obedient. This shows she is ambitious."*

Rewrite this as one integrated sentence or two, so that the context explains the effect of the quotation.
question.hint: Use a 'so that' or 'would have' move: what would a Jacobean audience feel about a woman asking to be stripped of her femininity, and why does Shakespeare make her ask for it?
question.explanation: A strong rewrite: Lady Macbeth's plea to be unsexed rejects the gentleness and obedience expected of a Jacobean wife, so that an audience raised on those expectations would have found her not merely ambitious but unnatural, which is exactly the horror Shakespeare needs to make her later collapse feel like nature reasserting itself.

markScheme.criterion: Keeps the quotation and links the context directly to it rather than stating the context separately
Explains the effect on the original audience (shock, unnatural, horror, transgression)
Connects the context to Shakespeare's purpose or to a later development (her collapse, the sleepwalking, the natural order)

question.text:
Read this extract from Act 1 Scene 3 of *Macbeth*. Banquo speaks after the witches' prophecy about Macbeth has partly come true.

> BANQUO: But 'tis strange: / And oftentimes, to win us to our harm, / The instruments of darkness tell us truths, / Win us with honest trifles, to betray's / In deepest consequence.

Write ONE paragraph on how Shakespeare presents the danger of the witches here. Your paragraph must analyse the language and integrate at least two sentences of context that explain the effect on Shakespeare's original audience and on a modern audience.
question.hint: Language: 'instruments of darkness', 'honest trifles', 'betray', 'deepest consequence'. Context: James I and Daemonologie; the belief that the devil tempts through half-truths; the Gunpowder Plot and equivocation; modern readings of the witches as psychological.
question.explanation: A strong paragraph analyses 'instruments of darkness' as making the witches tools of a greater evil, 'honest trifles' as the oxymoronic bait, and 'deepest consequence' as damnation; links this to James I's belief in witches as the devil's servants and to the Jacobean fear of equivocation after the Gunpowder Plot; contrasts a modern reading in which the witches voice Macbeth's own desires; and explains that Shakespeare's equivocal witches serve both audiences.

markScheme.criterion: Analyses 'instruments of darkness' as presenting the witches as tools of a larger evil or the devil
Analyses 'honest trifles' or 'betray' as showing how small truths are used as bait for great harm
Integrates context about James I, Daemonologie or Jacobean belief in witches as tempters to explain the original audience's fear
Integrates context about equivocation or the Gunpowder Plot, or about the Divine Right and regicide, tied to the language
Offers a modern reading (the witches as psychological, as Macbeth's own desire, or as a study of manipulation) contrasted with the original
Explains Shakespeare's purpose or the dramatic effect of Banquo's warning (dramatic irony, foreshadowing, contrast with Macbeth's reaction)

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- AO3 rewards the **relationship** between text and context: a fact becomes context only when it explains a **writer's choice** or a **reader's response**.
- Kinds of context: **historical, social, religious and philosophical, literary, biographical, reception**. Distinguish **production** from **reception**.
- Learn **three or four** precise ideas per text (James I and Divine Right; the Poor Law and Malthus; 1912 versus 1945; Romanticism and war).
- Integrate with the **so that**, **would have**, **then and now**, **purpose** and **form** moves; place context **after** analysis of a quotation.
- Avoid **bolt-ons**, **biography dumps**, **generalisations**, **anachronism**, **over-claiming** and context in **unseen poetry**.
- AO3 is **6 of 30** marks: brief, specific, integrated.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 can be used as context for *Macbeth*, and give one specific moment in the play it helps to illuminate.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about treason, the killing of a king, equivocation, and how a 1606 audience would feel watching a regicide.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Gunpowder Plot was a failed attempt to kill James I and Parliament, so a 1606 audience would have been intensely aware of the horror of treason against a king. This illuminates Duncan's murder and the unnatural chaos that follows, or the Porter's reference to an equivocator, which alludes to the trials of the plotters, or Macbeth's own fear of equivocating prophecies in Act 5.

markScheme.criterion: Explains what the Gunpowder Plot was (a plot to kill James I / treason against the king)
Explains how it shaped the audience's response to regicide or to equivocation
Names a specific moment (Duncan's murder and its aftermath, the Porter's equivocator, Macbeth's realisation that the prophecies equivocate)

practiceQuestions.text:
Read this extract from Stave One of *A Christmas Carol*, where Marley's ghost describes his chain:

> "I wear the chain I forged in life," replied the Ghost. "I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will, and of my own free will I wore it."

Write ONE paragraph on how Dickens presents responsibility here, integrating context about Victorian religious belief and about attitudes to wealth so that it explains the effect of the language.
practiceQuestions.hint: Language: 'forged', 'link by link', the repetition of 'my own free will'. Context: Christian ideas of judgement and free will; the chain made of cash-boxes; Victorian celebration of self-made wealth turned into self-made damnation.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong paragraph analyses 'forged' and 'link by link' as making sin a gradual craft, and the repeated 'my own free will' as insisting on personal responsibility; links this to Christian belief in judgement and free will that Dickens's readers shared; notes that the chain of cash-boxes turns the Victorian pride in self-made wealth into self-made punishment; and explains Dickens's purpose in warning prosperous readers.

markScheme.criterion: Analyses 'forged' or 'link by link, and yard by yard' as presenting sin or greed as gradual, self-made work
Analyses the repetition of 'my own free will' as insisting on personal responsibility
Integrates Christian context (judgement, punishment after death, free will) to explain the effect on Victorian readers
Integrates context about Victorian attitudes to wealth (the self-made man, cash-boxes, business) turned into punishment
Explains Dickens's purpose or the effect on the reader (warning to the prosperous; Scrooge's chain already longer)

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a paragraph of biography about the writer's childhood, placed at the start of an essay, is a reliable way to secure AO3 marks.
practiceQuestions.hint: Ask whether the biography explains any specific choice in the text.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Biography that is not tied to a choice in the text earns little or nothing. Context is rewarded when it explains why a writer made a decision or how an audience responds.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text:
A student writes: *"Scrooge asks 'Are there no prisons?' In Victorian times there were workhouses. This shows he is mean."*

Rewrite this as one integrated sentence or two, so that the context explains the effect of the quotation.
practiceQuestions.hint: Use a 'so that' or 'would have' move: what would a Victorian reader recognise in Scrooge's question, and why does Dickens give him these words?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong rewrite: Scrooge's question 'Are there no prisons?' echoes the harsh logic of the 1834 Poor Law, which treated poverty as a crime to be punished in workhouses, so that Dickens's readers would have recognised in Scrooge not a monster but a common attitude, which is exactly why the Ghost of Christmas Present later throws the words back at him.

markScheme.criterion: Keeps the quotation and links the context directly to it rather than stating the context separately
Explains the effect on the reader (recognition of a common attitude, shock, Dickens's criticism of it)
Connects the context to Dickens's purpose or to a later development (the words thrown back, Ignorance and Want, Scrooge's transformation)

practiceQuestions.text:
Read this extract from Act 1 Scene 4 of *Macbeth*. Duncan speaks about the Thane of Cawdor, who has just been executed for treason.

> DUNCAN: There's no art / To find the mind's construction in the face: / He was a gentleman on whom I built / An absolute trust.

Write ONE paragraph on how Shakespeare presents the danger of trusting appearances here. Your paragraph must analyse the language and integrate at least two sentences of context that explain the effect on Shakespeare's original audience and on a modern audience.
practiceQuestions.hint: Language: 'no art', 'the mind's construction in the face', 'built', 'absolute trust', and the fact that Macbeth enters on the next line. Context: the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 and betrayal by trusted subjects; the Divine Right of Kings and the vulnerability of a trusting monarch; modern audiences and political image-making.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong paragraph analyses 'no art' and 'the mind's construction in the face' as admitting that faces cannot be read, with the building metaphor of 'built' and 'construction' showing trust as a structure that can collapse; notes the dramatic irony of 'absolute trust' as Macbeth, the next traitor, enters; links this to the Jacobean fear of hidden treason after the Gunpowder Plot, and to the Divine Right that made a king's misplaced trust so dangerous; contrasts a modern reading in which the lines speak to political spin and manipulation; and explains that Shakespeare uses Duncan's blindness to foreshadow the theme of false faces.

markScheme.criterion: Analyses 'no art' or 'the mind's construction in the face' as showing that faces cannot be read, or the building metaphor of trust
Analyses 'absolute trust' or 'gentleman' and the irony that Macbeth enters as Duncan speaks
Integrates context about the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 or fear of treason by trusted subjects to explain the original audience's response
Integrates context about the Divine Right of Kings or regicide, tied to Duncan's vulnerability
Offers a modern reading (political image-making, manipulation, appearance and reality today) contrasted with the original
Explains Shakespeare's purpose or the dramatic effect (foreshadowing, dramatic irony, the false face motif, appearance versus reality)
